strengths: Soundness: The central systems intuition is plausible and empirically motivated: only about 2–4 of 32 block tokens are typically decoded per step, and the early-layer attention-delta signal consistently ranks decodable tokens above alternatives across several tasks and model families.

Evaluation: The paper reports broad quality results on five benchmarks and throughput measurements on two substantially different block-diffusion models. The Top/Random/Bottom comparison, cache ablation, block-size study, and processed-to-decoded-token ratios provide useful supporting evidence.

Significance: Reducing query-side computation in diffusion language models addresses an important deployment bottleneck. The reported 2.32× gain at block size 32 and 3.52× gain at block size 64 would be practically meaningful if validated under fully controlled settings.

Originality: Using early-layer changes in incoming attention to predict decodability, then compacting the remaining transformer computation, is a novel and interesting adaptation of attention-based sparsification to DLLM inference.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear, and its diagrams, pseudocode, kernel descriptions, and scheduler discussion make the proposed system understandable. Ethics: This is primarily an efficiency contribution and presents no apparent material ethical concern beyond the ordinary dual-use and environmental impacts of facilitating LLM deployment.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline throughput comparison is insufficiently controlled. Section 5.2 adopts confidence 0.8 and α=1.5 for FOCUS, whereas the stated default in Section 5 is confidence 0.9; Section 5.3 does not clearly specify the settings used by each system. Confidence thresholds directly affect both decoding parallelism and quality, so the reported speedups cannot be interpreted reliably without matched-quality, matched-threshold comparisons or a quality–throughput Pareto curve.

Soundness: The strongest 3.52× result is obtained at block size 64, but generation quality is evaluated only at the default block size 32. Because eviction and approximate intra-block caching can alter outputs, the paper has not established that its largest acceleration preserves quality.

Evaluation: Throughput is measured only on one A100 GPU, without latency distributions, time-to-first-token, GPU utilization/roofline profiles, memory use, or serving-SLO results. The claim that DLLMs are fundamentally compute-bound is supported mainly by FLOP accounting and a throughput plateau, not direct hardware profiling across devices.

Evaluation: The benchmarking script terminates requests exhibiting “excessive repetition,” but the detection rule and its incidence per method are not reported. Since FOCUS changes generation behavior, method-dependent early termination could materially bias tokens/second. Input/output-length statistics and the precise throughput denominator are also missing.

Theory: Appendix D does not validate eviction safety. It assumes unverified Gaussian classes with equal variance and γ>1, reports neither fitted parameters nor goodness-of-fit, and yields a bound that can be nearly one. It analyzes a σ threshold even though the algorithm performs top-K selection with a history-dependent budget, and therefore neither proves the actual procedure safe nor shows that it “minimizes” missed decodable tokens.

Internal consistency: Eq. 5 and Algorithm 1 count tokens satisfying ΔI≥Std(ΔI), while the implementation appendix says the kernel applies ΔI>μ+σ. The text alternates between a cumulative and an exponential moving average for the historical budget. These discrepancies affect the implemented algorithm and reproducibility.

Evidence: Quality tables provide point estimates only. Results are averaged over merely two runs, with no variation, significance analysis, decoding seeds, or discussion of whether observed gains such as 0.5–3 points exceed evaluation noise. Some quality improvements attributed to filtering incorrect tokens therefore remain speculative.

Baselines: The Fast-dLLM v2 comparison changes both inference framework and model size, as the authors acknowledge, so its 9.04× result does not isolate algorithmic benefit. Against LMDeploy, FOCUS additionally includes neighbor-aware caching and extensive custom kernels; Figure 8 helps, but a matched implementation of token eviction alone and clearer accounting of all baseline features are still needed.

Reproducibility: Despite extensive qualitative implementation detail and a claim of public code, the manuscript provides no visible repository URL or artifact reference, exact dependency/commit versions, complete decoding parameters and prompts, repetition-termination rule, warm-up protocol, or variance in timing. Reproducing the headline numbers would be difficult.

Limitations and presentation: The paper lacks a substantive limitations section. It does not adequately discuss dependence on attention accessibility, early-layer signal quality, block-diffusion architecture, irregular-kernel support, small retained workloads, other accelerators, or workloads where disabling LMDeploy’s multi-loop optimization causes regressions. Claims of a “universal” MDLM characteristic and “fundamentally” compute-bound inference exceed the evidence from the tested systems.

strengths: Originality: FOCUS introduces an interesting training-free use of early-layer attention-delta signals for query-token eviction, adapting sparsity ideas to the compute bottleneck of block-diffusion language models.

Significance: Reducing redundant computation in diffusion-LLM serving is practically important. The reported throughput gains over LMDeploy are substantial—up to 2.32× at the default block size and 3.52× at block size 64.

Soundness: The paper evaluates two materially different block-diffusion architectures, SDAR-8B-Chat and the MoE LLaDA2.0-mini, and covers mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and serving workloads.

The Top/Random/Bottom selection comparison provides useful evidence that the proposed importance signal carries information beyond an arbitrary retention policy. Ablations also separate intra-block caching from the full system.
Presentation: The motivation, system overview, pseudocode, kernel descriptions, and throughput figures are generally clear and make the proposed implementation understandable at a high level.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed theoretical safety result does not establish safety of the implemented method. It assumes equal-variance Gaussian class-conditional distributions without validating that assumption; uses the standard deviation of the non-decodable distribution, whereas Eq. 5 computes a statistic over all masked tokens; and analyzes a fixed threshold although the implementation retains a top-K set under additional constraints. It also treats a false negative only as lost parallelism, overlooking that stale or missing intermediate states can change logits and future generations. Consequently, the claims that the bound validates the algorithm and is strictly conservative are unsupported.

Soundness: The exact computational semantics are insufficiently specified. After Layer 1, evicted tokens are said to remain as fixed reference KV states, but transformer layers have distinct K/V projections and the manuscript does not clearly explain where valid layer-specific states for evicted, still-masked tokens come from. Reusing states from earlier denoising steps would be approximate rather than the exact caching advertised in Table 1. The interaction among eviction, placeholder initialization, delayed caching, and later-layer attention needs a precise derivation or equivalence argument.

Evaluation: The throughput comparison does not clearly report the confidence threshold and all decoding settings used for each system. FOCUS adopts confidence 0.8 and alpha 1.5 after comparing its average quality with the baseline at confidence 0.9, so the speedup may combine token eviction with a more aggressive decoding policy. Per-task quality is not uniformly preserved: for example, this FOCUS setting trails the 0.9 baseline on Math500 and HumanEval. Matched-policy and matched-quality throughput curves are required to isolate the contribution.

Evaluation: Claims of preserving or improving quality are too strong given the evidence. Results are averaged over only two runs, with no uncertainty, significance tests, paired output analysis, or worst-case degradation characterization. Table 6 itself shows that the proposed neighbor-aware cache alone still lowers several scores. Average benchmark performance cannot rule out systematic failures caused by approximate state reuse.

Systems evidence is too narrow for the broad production and compute-bound claims. All measurements use one A100 GPU; there are no roofline measurements, FLOP/kernel breakdowns, latency or time-to-first-token results, memory usage, request-length distributions, or experiments on newer/different accelerators. The approximately 1% overhead assertion is reported without detailed measurements. Repetition-based early termination may also affect workload comparability and is not quantified.

The Fast-dLLM v2 comparison is substantially confounded: the methods use different models and serving stacks, and the paper attributes much of the 9.04× gap to continuous batching and PagedAttention missing from the baseline. This does not isolate the proposed eviction technique and should not be presented as direct algorithmic superiority.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a systems contribution. The paper claims a public GitHub implementation and more than 4,000 lines of custom code but provides no accessible repository reference in the manuscript, commit, environment versions, complete benchmark commands, sampled request identifiers, or detailed per-component profiles. Several implementation descriptions are internally inconsistent, including cumulative versus exponential moving averages and CUDA-graph support that is described extensively but disabled in all throughput experiments.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement is boilerplate, and there is no dedicated discussion of failure modes, approximation-induced output changes, hardware dependence, workload-specific behavior, or privacy considerations for ShareGPT/WildChat. The ethical risk is limited for an inference optimization, but the treatment of limitations is not adequate. Overall, the idea is promising, but unresolved correctness, comparison, and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Soundness: The central systems idea is plausible and supported by substantial evidence. Across SDAR and LLaDA2.0, early-layer attention-importance deltas consistently concentrate decodable tokens in the highest percentile, and Top-K selection decisively outperforms random and bottom-K controls.

Significance: FOCUS addresses an important deployment bottleneck for diffusion language models. On an A100, it reduces the reported processed-to-decoded-token ratio by roughly 64–80% and improves throughput over LMDeploy by up to 2.32x at block size 32 and 3.52x at block size 64.

Originality: Repurposing attention importance from KV-cache compression to within-block query-token eviction is a useful conceptual contribution. Dynamic budgeting, structural retention constraints, neighbor-aware caching, and sparse Triton kernels form a coherent system.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized. Figures 2–8 explain the motivation, predictor, system, quality results, and throughput scaling effectively; the appendix provides pseudocode and unusually extensive implementation details.

The evaluation spans mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, real-world chat, dense and MoE models, several confidence thresholds, and multiple block and batch sizes. The comparison to an optimized LMDeploy baseline is more meaningful than comparison only to research prototypes.

Reproducibility is promising: the authors state that the system is publicly available and describe the hardware, principal settings, evaluation frameworks, scheduler state, custom kernels, cache policy, and CUDA-graph configuration. No material ethical concern is apparent; the work may reduce inference compute.
weaknesses: Soundness: The quality-preservation claim is not established at a controlled speed–quality operating point. FOCUS changes the effective decoding schedule, so comparing methods at the same confidence threshold is not necessarily fair; conversely, the highlighted default compares FOCUS at threshold 0.8 against the baseline at 0.9. Curves matching accuracy against throughput or latency are needed.

There is an important internal inconsistency in Table 6. Its FOCUS row exactly matches the alpha=1.5, confidence=0.8 row of Table 4, although the surrounding ablation discussion states that the confidence threshold is fixed at 0.9. This weakens the claimed cache ablation and the assertion that the complete system surpasses the baseline under comparable settings.

The theoretical analysis is much weaker than advertised. It assumes equal-variance Gaussian class-conditional distributions and SNR greater than one without estimating or testing these assumptions. Moreover, the bound analyzes thresholding at one standard deviation, whereas Algorithm 1 ultimately uses a Top-K rule with a history-dependent budget. It therefore neither proves eviction safety nor justifies claims that the method minimizes error.

The empirical correlation analysis reports percentile histograms rather than direct predictor metrics such as recall of decodable tokens, precision–recall/AUROC, false-negative rate, or recall versus retained-token budget. Such measurements are especially important because missed candidates can change the iterative trajectory.

The strongest throughput evidence is limited to one A100 GPU, averages only two runs, and provides no variability, latency percentiles, memory consumption, output-length statistics, or completed-request counts. The benchmark also terminates excessively repetitive requests; without per-method termination rates, this policy could bias tokens/s. Generalization to newer GPUs and multi-GPU serving remains unknown.

Generation-quality coverage is uneven: the detailed end-to-end threshold study is only for SDAR, while the second architecture mainly appears in selection and throughput experiments. Several benchmark differences are small, but uncertainty or significance estimates are absent, so claims of quality improvement are stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix: exact software/model revisions, seeds, prompt and decoding configurations, request-length distributions, and complete profiling methodology are not reported. The main text and appendix also differ between a standard-deviation threshold and a mean-plus-standard-deviation implementation description.

Presentation occasionally overstates scope: results on three related masked-diffusion models do not establish that the correlation is a universal intrinsic characteristic of MDLMs, and the compute-bound characterization is not backed by a roofline or hardware-counter analysis. Limitations are scattered rather than explicitly discussed, particularly the single-hardware evaluation, model-family scope, and disabled LMDeploy multi-loop optimization.

The impact statement is boilerplate. Although no major ethical issue is evident, a short discussion of energy implications and the privacy/provenance considerations of ShareGPT and WildChat would be more appropriate.

strengths: Soundness: The central systems idea is plausible and supported by substantial evidence. Across SDAR and LLaDA2.0, FOCUS reduces the reported processed-to-decoded-token ratio by roughly 64–80% (Table 5) and delivers consistent end-to-end throughput gains on A100 and H100 GPUs, including an engine-controlled comparison with Fast-dLLM v2.

Significance: Compute-efficient serving is an important obstacle for diffusion language models. The reported gains are practically meaningful—up to 2.32× at the default block size and 3.52× at block size 64—and the method improves scaling at high concurrency rather than only optimizing batch-size-1 latency.

Originality: Using the change in incoming attention importance between the first two layers to predict token decodability, followed by intra-block query-token eviction, is a novel and interesting departure from prior KV-cache eviction methods.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and polished. It explains the bottleneck, selection mechanism, cache policy, custom kernels, scheduler, and CUDA-graph considerations in considerable detail, with useful pseudocode and extensive appendices.

The evaluation covers mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and serving workloads; two distinct DLLM architectures, multiple block sizes and expansion factors, and two GPU generations are tested. The authors also honestly report batch-size-1 regressions and qualify their proposed explanation for quality improvements as non-causal.
No material research-ethics concern is apparent: this is an inference-efficiency technique evaluated on established models and benchmarks.
weaknesses: The main throughput comparison is not sufficiently controlled for decoding behavior. Section 5.2 selects confidence 0.8 for FOCUS, whereas the stated standard/default baseline setting is 0.9, and Section 5.3 does not unambiguously specify each method’s threshold. Because confidence directly changes both decoded-token yield, quality, and runtime, the headline speedups need matched-threshold and matched-quality comparisons on every serving workload. Figure 16 provides a useful quality–throughput frontier only for GSM8K and does not resolve this issue for ShareGPT, WildChat, or MATH.

The evidence for the predictor is incomplete. The percentile plots show enrichment rather than near-perfect separation—the top 20% contains only about 52–62% of decodable tokens in many settings—but the paper does not report AUROC, precision/recall, missed-decodable-token rate, or how these quantities vary by step and workload. Such measurements are particularly important because predictor errors alter the diffusion trajectory.

Appendix D does not provide a meaningful safety guarantee for the implemented algorithm. Its Gaussian, equal-variance, and positive-shift assumptions are asserted rather than tested; the signal-to-noise ratio is not estimated; and the derivation analyzes a fixed one-standard-deviation decision rule, whereas the actual method retains a top-K set determined jointly by N_sigma, historical decoding counts, and structural constraints. Calling this a theoretical validation that minimizes missed tokens is therefore overstated.

The claim that non-decoded tokens represent approximately 90% wasted computation is stronger than established. In a bidirectional diffusion block, representations of tokens that are not unmasked on the current step can still influence retained tokens. FOCUS changes or reuses these states rather than proving their computation semantically unnecessary. The manuscript should more precisely distinguish current-step decoding yield from causal computational redundancy and clarify exactly which stale/fixed KV states remain visible after eviction.

Important design components lack controlled ablations: dynamic versus static budgeting, delta versus raw Layer-1 importance in end-to-end quality and speed, AR-context preservation, placeholder integrity, and their interactions with neighbor-aware caching. Table 6 partly studies caching, but DC+ itself remains below the baseline on four of five quality benchmarks, making it difficult to attribute the full system’s quality recovery.

Reproducibility is presently limited. The paper describes more than 4,000 lines of custom LMDeploy/Triton code but provides no code or artifact availability statement, dependency and commit versions, random seeds, sampled request IDs, prompt/output-length distributions, or exact repetition-termination rule. Terminating requests with “excessive repetition” can materially bias throughput unless termination rates and identical handling across methods are reported.

Results are averaged over only two runs without dispersion or confidence intervals. This makes small accuracy differences and some throughput differences difficult to interpret. The accuracy hyperparameter alpha is also selected using the same benchmark results on which the final quality claim is made, with no validation/test separation.

The systems evaluation emphasizes aggregate tokens per second but omits latency distributions, time-to-first-token, per-request completion time, memory consumption, and performance under arrival traces or latency SLOs. Comparisons with other recent caching systems discussed in related work are also absent. These omissions reduce the strength of the production-serving claims.

The limitations and impact discussions are thin relative to the scope of the claims. The paper acknowledges low-batch regressions and immature DLLM infrastructure, but should also discuss model-specific attention behavior, altered generation trajectories, benchmark-level hyperparameter tuning, hardware/kernel portability, and the limited evidence for full-diffusion deployment.

strengths: The paper identifies an important systems bottleneck in diffusion LLM inference: full-block computation produces only about 2–4 decoded tokens per step at block size 32. The proposed early-layer token eviction directly targets this redundancy. The systems contribution is meaningful and reasonably original: FOCUS combines an early-layer attention-delta signal, dynamic retention budgets, structural safeguards, neighbor-aware intra-block caching, and specialized Triton kernels. Query-token eviction within the current diffusion block is usefully distinguished from prior KV-cache eviction and reuse methods.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial. At the standard block size of 32, FOCUS reaches up to 2.32× the LMDeploy throughput; at block size 64 it reaches 3.52×. Results cover two block-diffusion architectures, three workload distributions, batch sizes from 32 to 256, and both A100 and H100 GPUs. An engine-controlled Fast-dLLM v2 comparison helps separate algorithmic gains from framework differences.

The evaluation includes useful ablations and sensitivity analyses: top/random/bottom selection, confidence threshold and expansion-factor sweeps, intra-block-cache variants, block-size effects, computational redundancy, batch-size-1 performance, and a quality–throughput frontier.

Presentation is generally polished and the appendices provide extensive implementation detail and pseudocode. The authors also honestly disclose regimes where FOCUS is slower, including most batch-size-1 settings, and discuss scheduler and multi-loop limitations.
The work introduces no material new ethical concern beyond the standard risks of making language-model deployment cheaper; the limited impact statement is therefore not itself a reason for rejection.
weaknesses: The central predictor evidence is not reported in the right statistical form. Figures 4, 12, and 13 appear to show the distribution of percentile bins conditioned on decodable/non-decodable class, although the text describes conditional decoding probability. They do not establish precision, recall, false-negative rate, AUROC/AUPRC, or recall@K under the actual dynamic budget. Consequently, claims that the signal is “robust,” “architecture-agnostic,” or “universal” are stronger than the presented evidence.

The theoretical safety analysis does not validate the implemented algorithm. It assumes equal-variance Gaussians, a known non-decodable mean and variance, and signal-to-noise ratio greater than one, without fitting or testing these assumptions. More importantly, its threshold uses the non-decodable distribution, whereas Eq. 5 computes a standard deviation over the whole block and the algorithm retains top-K tokens with K also controlled by history and structural constraints. The resulting Mills-ratio bound therefore does not apply directly to FOCUS, and no measured SNR or empirical error-bound comparison is supplied. Claims of optimality and a “strictly conservative” bound are unsupported.

The manuscript contains material specification inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 selects top-K according to Eq. 4, while Appendix E.2.2 describes direct selection above a blockwise mean-plus-standard-deviation threshold. The local dependency is variously described as ti depending on ti−1 and as ti depending on ti+1. Placeholder Integrity can retain every masked token preceding the rightmost selected candidate, but the paper does not characterize how this changes the effective budget or explain why it does not usually erase the intended sparsity.

Generation quality is evaluated through a Hugging Face backend, whereas throughput uses the heavily modified LMDeploy implementation. Thus the quality tables do not directly validate the exact optimized path containing custom ragged attention, sparse cache writes, state compaction, and asynchronous scheduler logic. End-to-end equivalence or quality measurements from the deployed engine are needed.

Quality results are single point estimates with no uncertainty, despite several claimed improvements being only a few percentage points. Throughput is averaged over only two runs without variability. The benchmark also terminates requests exhibiting “excessive repetition” but neither defines the rule nor reports termination rates by method; because the methods can differ in repetition behavior, this may bias throughput comparisons.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a system whose claimed implementation exceeds 4,000 lines. The manuscript provides no artifact or code link and omits software versions, commits, seeds, detailed decoding settings, the sampled request set, and sufficient information to reproduce custom kernels and the repetition filter. Pseudocode and kernel descriptions are helpful but cannot substitute for the implementation.

The scope of the strongest conclusions is too broad. Evidence comes primarily from two related block-diffusion models and high-concurrency single-GPU serving. FOCUS is slower on most batch-size-1 cases—substantially so on MATH—and no latency distributions, memory costs, multi-GPU results, or production traces are reported. These limitations narrow the practical significance of claims about scalable or production deployment.

Overall, the idea and reported speedups are promising, but the mismatch between the claimed theory and actual selection rule, incomplete predictor validation, separation of quality and optimized-engine evaluation, and missing reproducibility artifact prevent others from reliably establishing the central claims. A revision with direct detection metrics, controlled engine-level quality tests, statistical uncertainty, reconciled algorithm definitions, and released code could become competitive.

strengths: Soundness: The central systems result is supported by substantial end-to-end evidence. On A100 and H100 GPUs, FOCUS improves large-batch throughput across SDAR and LLaDA2.0, three workload datasets, multiple batch sizes, and block sizes 16–64; the engine-controlled Fast-dLLM v2 comparison is particularly valuable.

Originality: Using the change in incoming attention importance between the first two layers to predict token decodability and evict query tokens within the current diffusion block is a novel and well-motivated departure from prior KV-cache eviction methods.

Significance: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in diffusion-language-model serving. Reducing the processed-to-decoded-token ratio by roughly 64–80% and obtaining up to 2.32x speedup at the standard block size, with 3.52x at block size 64, would be useful if the implementation is released.

Evaluation: The authors include informative selection controls, hyperparameter sweeps, a quality–throughput frontier, component ablations, low-concurrency results, two model architectures, and an additional GPU generation. They also fairly disclose that FOCUS can regress at batch size 1 and explain the disabled multi-loop optimization.

Presentation and limitations: The paper is generally clear, visually polished, and unusually detailed about kernels, scheduling, cache state, and CUDA-graph handling. It appropriately presents the proposed explanation for quality improvements as indirect rather than established causal evidence, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical “eviction safety” result is much weaker than advertised. It assumes Gaussian class-conditional deltas with equal variance and gamma>1 without validating these assumptions or estimating gamma. Moreover, the implementation uses the block-wide standard deviation and a top-K budget, whereas the derivation uses the non-decodable-class variance and a fixed threshold. The claim that the bound is strictly conservative is therefore not established.

The predictor analysis lacks direct classification metrics such as decodable-token recall, precision, AUROC, and false-negative rate. Percentile histograms and Top/Random/Bottom generation results establish useful association, but do not fully substantiate claims that the signal is robust, architecture-agnostic, or universal.

The generation-quality evidence is incomplete for the full system. The main threshold/alpha comparison and cache ablation cover only SDAR, while LLaDA2.0 appears mainly in fixed-budget selection and throughput experiments. Reported quality differences have no uncertainty or significance analysis, and averaging only two efficiency runs without variance leaves measurement stability unclear.

The serving evaluation reports aggregate token throughput but omits latency distributions, time to first token, per-request completion latency, memory usage, and fairness under mixed request lengths. The benchmark also terminates requests with “excessive repetition” without specifying the rule or reporting termination rates; because FOCUS can alter generated content, this could confound throughput comparisons.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for a 4,000-plus-line systems contribution: the manuscript provides no code or artifact link, commit hashes, software versions, complete commands/configurations, or detailed prompt and dataset preprocessing. There is also ambiguity about whether the principal throughput experiments use confidence 0.8 or 0.9 because different sections state different defaults. These issues should be resolved before others can reliably reproduce the headline results.
